what_its_for: Ceftriaxone is an antibiotic used to treat many types of bacterial infections, including pneumonia, skin infections, urinary tract infections, ear infections, meningitis (infection of the brain lining), and certain sexually transmitted infections like gonorrhea. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection.
how_to_take: Ceftriaxone is given as an injection or IV (into a vein) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. You will NOT give this medication to yourself at home unless a healthcare provider has specifically trained you to do so. Each injection or infusion usually takes about 30 minutes. Do not skip any scheduled doses or appointments, as finishing the full course of treatment is very important to make sure the infection is completely gone.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on your age, weight, the type of infection you have, and how serious it is. Adults usually receive 1 to 2 grams once or twice a day. Children's doses are based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. Do not stop treatment early, even if you start feeling better.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled infusion or injection appointment, contact your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Skipping doses can make your infection harder to treat and may allow the bacteria to become resistant to the antibiotic.
storage: Ceftriaxone is stored and prepared by pharmacy or healthcare staff. If you are receiving home infusion therapy, store the prepared medication in the refrigerator as directed by your pharmacist. Keep it out of reach of children. Do not freeze unless specifically instructed. Use the medication before the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you drink alcohol regularly, as some antibiotics can interact with alcohol. Avoid taking calcium-containing products (like antacids or IV fluids with calcium) at the same time as ceftriaxone, especially in newborns, as this can be dangerous. Do not take any new medications, vitamins, or supplements without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of your face, lips, or throat, trouble breathing, or dizziness; severe or watery diarrhea (which may be a sign of a serious gut infection called C. diff); yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); severe stomach pain; signs of kidney problems such as little or no urination; unusual bruising or bleeding; or any new or worsening symptoms during treatment.
when_it_works: Many people start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting ceftriaxone. However, it is very important to complete the full course of treatment your doctor prescribed, even if you feel well before it is finished. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back and may make it harder to treat in the future.
special_populations: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning to become pregnant, as your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks. Newborns and premature babies need special monitoring because ceftriaxone can interact with calcium and cause serious problems. Older adults and people with kidney or liver disease may need dose adjustments and closer monitoring. Always mention all your medical conditions and medications to your healthcare team.
